content.text:
An object on Earth has a weight of $490\,\mathrm{N}$ and experiences an acceleration due to gravity of $9.8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. On Mars, this object would experience an acceleration due to gravity of $3.7\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

On Mars, what would be the weight of this object?
$490\,\mathrm{N}$
$\dfrac{490}{9.8}\,\mathrm{N}$
$\dfrac{490}{9.8}\times 3.7\,\mathrm{N}$
$\dfrac{490}{3.7}\times 9.8\,\mathrm{N}$
Weight is $W = mg$, so you need the mass of the object before you can find its weight anywhere.
Get the mass from the data given for Earth, then combine it with the acceleration due to gravity on Mars. Which single option performs both steps in the right order?
C
Find the mass of the object from the information given for Earth.
The mass is unchanged on Mars, but the acceleration due to gravity is different, so the weight changes.
Written without the intermediate step this is $W_{\mathrm{Mars}} = \frac{490}{9.8}\times 3.7\,\mathrm{N}$, which is option C.
Option A keeps the weight at its Earth value, option B leaves the $g$ on Earth in place of the value for Mars, and option D inverts the ratio of the two accelerations.

content.text: Which of these statements best describes the forces acting on a satellite in orbit around Earth?
Although gravity has no effect, there is still an outward force.
The satellite is kept up by an outward force that balances the force due to gravity.
Gravity is the only force acting on the satellite and this results in an inward acceleration.
The effect of gravity is negligible, the satellite is kept in orbit by its momentum and the net force on it is zero.
A satellite moving along a circular orbit has a velocity whose direction changes continuously, so its acceleration is not zero and there must be a non-zero net force on it.

Use $a = \frac{v^{2}}{r}$ to find the direction of that acceleration, then ask which force is available to provide it. No force is required to 'keep the satellite up' — check whether such a force appears in the options.
C

The velocity of the satellite is continually changing direction, so there is a non-zero acceleration and therefore a non-zero net force. A zero net force is impossible, which rules out D, and gravity is plainly not negligible, which rules out A.
Because $a = \frac{v^{2}}{r}$ is directed towards the centre of the circular orbit, the net force must be directed inwards, towards Earth. Nothing pushes the satellite outwards, so B is wrong.
Gravity is the only force acting on the satellite, and it produces that inward (centripetal) acceleration. Option C.

An aeroplane is flying horizontally over level ground. It has an altitude of $490\,\mathrm{m}$ and a velocity of $100\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. As the aeroplane passes directly above a cross marked on the ground, an object is released from the aeroplane.

How far away from the cross will this object land?
$490\,\mathrm{m}$

Treat the horizontal and vertical motion of the object separately. There is no horizontal force once it has left the aeroplane, so its horizontal velocity is unchanged, while the vertical motion is free fall from rest.
Find the time of fall from $s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^{2}$ with $u = 0$, then multiply that time by the constant horizontal velocity to get the horizontal distance from the cross.
B
Vertical: the object is released from rest relative to the ground, so $u = 0$ and $h = \frac{1}{2}gt^{2}$.
Horizontal: there is no horizontal force, so the horizontal velocity stays at the aeroplane's value of $100\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ for the whole $10\,\mathrm{s}$.

Option B. Option A is the drop height itself, option C comes from squaring the velocity instead of multiplying by the time, and option D has used the height in metres as though it were the time in seconds.

content.text:
An investigation was performed to determine the acceleration due to gravity. A ball was dropped from various heights and the time it took to reach the ground from each height was measured. The results were graphed with the independent variable on the horizontal axis.

Which graph best represents the relationship between the variables?

Height is the independent variable (it is deliberately varied), so height belongs on the horizontal axis and time on the vertical axis. Time of fall increases with height but not linearly, since $t \propto \sqrt{h}$.

content.alt_text: Graph with Time on the vertical axis and Height on the horizontal axis: a concave-down increasing curve with four data points lying below it.
Graph with Time on the vertical axis and Height on the horizontal axis: a straight line with a positive gradient and four data points scattered off the line.
Graph with Height on the vertical axis and Time on the horizontal axis: an increasing curve that is concave up, with four data points lying on it.
Graph with Height on the vertical axis and Time on the horizontal axis: a straight line with a positive gradient and four data points scattered about the line.

content.text: Start from $s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^{2}$. The ball is dropped from rest, so $u = 0$ and the height fallen is $h = \frac{1}{2}gt^{2}$.

That relationship is not symmetric, so use it to decide which way the curve bends. Before choosing, ask which quantity the experimenter deliberately changed — that is the one that belongs on the horizontal axis.
A

Height is the quantity the experimenter deliberately varied, so it is the independent variable and belongs on the horizontal axis; the time of fall is the measured, dependent variable and belongs on the vertical axis. This alone rules out the two graphs with height on the vertical axis.

With $u = 0$, $h = \frac{1}{2}gt^{2}$, so $t = \sqrt{\frac{2h}{g}}$. Time therefore increases with height, but more slowly at large heights, giving a curve that rises steeply at first and then flattens out.

That is the graph in option A. Options B and D assume a straight line, which would mean the time increases in direct proportion to the height — the behaviour of constant velocity, not constant acceleration.

A spaceship is travelling away from Earth at $1.8\times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The time interval between consecutive ticks of a clock on board the spaceship is $0.50\,\mathrm{s}$. Each time the clock ticks, a radio pulse is transmitted back to Earth.

What is the time interval between consecutive radio pulses as measured on Earth?
The clock is at rest in the spaceship's frame of reference, so the interval between ticks is the proper time $t_0$.
Earth's observers see the spaceship moving, so they measure a dilated interval $t = \frac{t_0}{\sqrt{1 - v^{2}/c^{2}}}$. Express the speed as a fraction of $c$ before substituting.
C
Express the spaceship's speed as a fraction of the speed of light.
Earth's observers see the spaceship's clock running slow, so the interval they measure is longer than the proper interval $t_0 = 0.50\,\mathrm{s}$.

$t = 0.63\,\mathrm{s}$ to two significant figures, so option C. The dilation factor must exceed 1, which already eliminates A ($0.40\,\mathrm{s}$) and B ($0.50\,\mathrm{s}$); D is larger still and cannot be produced by the correct factor.

content.text:
Three identical wires $W_1$, $W_2$ and $W_3$ are positioned as shown. Each carries a current of the same magnitude in the direction indicated.

What is the magnitude and direction of the resultant force on $W_2$?

content.alt_text: Three parallel vertical wires W1, W2 and W3 evenly spaced, separated by distance d. Current in W1 and W3 points down the page; current in W2 points up the page.

content.text: Magnitude: Zero; Direction: None
Magnitude: Non zero; Direction: To the left
Magnitude: Non zero; Direction: To the right
Magnitude: Non zero; Direction: Out of the page
Two long parallel wires carrying currents in the same direction attract each other; currents in opposite directions repel. Apply that rule to $W_2$ once for $W_1$ and once for $W_3$.
Then compare the two forces: are the currents equal in magnitude, and is the separation from $W_2$ the same in both cases?
A

The current in $W_1$ runs opposite to the current in $W_2$, so $W_1$ repels $W_2$, pushing it away from $W_1$ — that is, to the right. The current in $W_3$ is also opposite to the current in $W_2$, so $W_3$ repels $W_2$ to the left.
The two forces have equal magnitude, since $F = \frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi r}$ and both the currents and the separation ($r = d$) are the same, but they act in opposite directions.

The resultant force on $W_2$ is therefore zero and has no direction. Option A. Options B and C each account for only one of the two wires, and D confuses the direction of a force with the direction of a current.

content.text: Which of the following is necessary for the operation of an AC induction motor?
A fixed magnetic field in the rotor
A direct current supply to the rotor
A changing magnetic field in the rotor
Split rings conducting current to the rotor

In a DC motor the rotor is connected to the supply through split rings and a commutator. In an induction motor there is no electrical connection to the rotor at all — ask how a current can then be produced in it.
Contrast a field that is fixed in time, like that of a permanent magnet, with one that alternates. Only the second can change the flux through the rotor and so induce a current in it.
C
The rotor of an AC induction motor is not connected to the supply: it has no brushes, no commutator and no split rings. That rules out A, B and D.

The alternating current in the stator (field) coils makes the magnetic field through the rotor change continuously, so the magnetic flux through the rotor changes with time and a current is induced in the rotor by electromagnetic induction.

The interaction between that induced current and the changing field produces the turning effect. A field that is fixed in time would change nothing, so the field in the rotor must be changing. Option C.

content.text:
A plastic cylinder with a metal strip, $M$, on its surface is rotated at constant speed about its axis, in a uniform magnetic field. During each rotation the strip, $M$, passes locations $W$, $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ shown below.

When is the potential difference across $M$ greatest?

content.alt_text: A plastic cylinder rotating clockwise about its horizontal axis between the N and S poles of a magnet. A metal strip M lies along the cylinder surface and passes through positions W (top left), X (right), Y (bottom) and Z (bottom left).

content.text: As $M$ passes $W$.
As $M$ passes $X$.
As $M$ passes $Y$.
As $M$ passes $Z$.
The potential difference across the strip is produced by the strip cutting field lines, so it depends on the component of the strip's velocity perpendicular to $B$: $|\varepsilon| = B\ell v_{\perp}$.

The field runs from $N$ to $S$, horizontally across the page, while the strip's speed is constant but its direction of motion is not. Work out the direction of the strip's instantaneous velocity as it reaches each of $W$, $X$, $Y$ and $Z$.
B

The potential difference across the strip is $|\varepsilon| = B\ell v_{\perp}$, where $v_{\perp}$ is the component of the strip's velocity perpendicular to the field, $\ell$ is the length of the strip and $B$ is constant.
The field runs from $N$ to $S$, horizontally across the page, so only the vertical component of the strip's velocity can cut field lines.

At $W$ (top of the cylinder) and at $Y$ (bottom) the strip is moving horizontally, parallel to $B$, so $v_{\perp} = 0$ and no potential difference is induced. At $Z$ the velocity is only partly vertical, so $v_{\perp}$ is less than its maximum value. At $X$ the strip is at the side of the cylinder and moving straight up or down, fully perpendicular to $B$, so $v_{\perp} = v$ and the potential difference is at its greatest.
Hence the potential difference across $M$ is greatest as $M$ passes $X$. Option B.

content.text: Which statement best explains how induction cooktops heat food?
Eddy currents generated in the water in the food produce heat.
Eddy currents generated in the base of the saucepan produce heat.
Resistance in the glass of the cooktop produces heat.
Resistance in the element beneath the glass cooktop produces heat.
Beneath the glass of an induction cooktop there is a coil carrying a rapidly alternating current, which produces a magnetic field that changes with time in the space above it.
Ask which conducting material actually sits in that changing field once the cooktop is switched on, and how the energy delivered to that material is dissipated.
B

The coil beneath the glass carries an alternating current and so produces an alternating magnetic field. The glass is an insulator and there is no resistive heating element under the glass, which rules out C and D, and the water in the food is not in the field, which rules out A.
The base of the iron saucepan is a conductor sitting in the changing magnetic field, so eddy currents are induced in it by electromagnetic induction.
The saucepan base has resistance, so the induced current dissipates electrical energy as thermal energy, which passes into the food and heats it. Option B.

content.text:
The cathode ray tube and transistor circuits in a conventional television rely on transformers.

What transformation of the $240\,\mathrm{V}$ AC input voltage do these components require?
Cathode ray tube: Step-up; Transistor circuits: Step-down
Cathode ray tube: Step-down; Transistor circuits: Step-up
Cathode ray tube: Step-up; Transistor circuits: Step-up
Cathode ray tube: Step-down; Transistor circuits: Step-down

Consider the voltage each part of a television needs. The electron gun in the cathode ray tube must accelerate electrons through the whole length of the tube, while the transistor circuits that run the set operate at low, safe voltage.
Recall which way a transformer changes voltage: $\frac{V_p}{V_s} = \frac{N_p}{N_s}$, so a step-down transformer must have more turns in the primary than in the secondary.
A

The cathode ray tube needs a potential difference of tens of thousands of volts to give the electrons enough kinetic energy to cross the tube, so its transformer must step the $240\,\mathrm{V}$ supply up.
The transistor circuits operate at low voltage, so their transformer must step the supply down, with more turns in the primary than in the secondary so that $V_p > V_s$.
Option A. Option B has both transformations the wrong way round, and options C and D apply the same transformation to both components, which is not what either component requires.

content.text:
An electron, $e$, moving with a velocity of $8.0\times 10^{6}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ enters a uniform magnetic field, $B$, of strength $2.1\times 10^{-2}\,\mathrm{T}$ as shown.

The electron experiences a force which causes it to move along a circular path. What is the radius of the path followed by the electron?

content.alt_text: A grid of crosses showing a uniform magnetic field B into the page. An electron e enters at 40 degrees to the field lines with a velocity arrow pointing up and to the right.

content.text: $1.1\times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}$
$1.4\times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}$
$1.7\times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}$
$2.2\times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}$

The crosses show the field directed into the plane of the page, while the electron's velocity lies in the plane of the page. Compare the angle between the velocity and $\mathbf{B}$ before using any trigonometry.
For a charged particle in a circular path the magnetic force supplies the centripetal force, so equate $qvB$ with $\frac{mv^{2}}{r}$ and rearrange for $r$. Note which quantities cancel.
D

The field is directed into the plane of the page and the velocity lies in the plane of the page, so the velocity is perpendicular to the field. The magnetic force $qvB$ is therefore the only force and is always perpendicular to the velocity, which is exactly the condition for a circular path. No $\sin\theta$ factor is needed, and the full speed enters the calculation.
Equate the magnetic force to the centripetal force.

Option D. The $40^{\circ}$ marked on the diagram is the angle through which the path is deflected, not the angle between the velocity and the field, so using it to reduce the velocity would be wrong. Options A, B and C all correspond to inserting an extra factor into the correct value.

content.text:
The debate as to whether cathode rays are charged particles or electromagnetic waves continued for many years.

Which observation of cathode rays resolved this debate?
Cathode rays can turn a paddle wheel.
An electric field can deflect cathode rays.
Cathode rays can penetrate thin metal foil.
Fluorescent screens glow when struck by cathode rays.

The debate was between cathode rays being a stream of charged particles and cathode rays being a form of electromagnetic wave. Decide which of the four observations could only be true of one of those two models.
Recall what happens when a charged particle enters an electric field, and compare that with the properties an electromagnetic wave would be expected to have.
B
An electromagnetic wave is uncharged and is not deflected by an electric field, so an observation of deflection establishes that cathode rays carry charge. That is option B.

Turning a paddle wheel (A) shows that the rays transfer energy and momentum, but an electromagnetic wave can do that too. Penetrating thin metal foil (C) is a property of penetrating radiation generally, and making a fluorescent screen glow (D) shows only that energy is transferred, not that the rays are charged.
Deflection by an electric field is the observation that resolved the debate, so option B is correct.

content.text:
When a magnet is released above a superconductor that has been cooled below its critical temperature, the magnet hovers above the superconductor. This is called the Meissner effect.

What is the best explanation for this?
The net force is zero due to electrostatic repulsion.
The magnetic field freezes at very low temperature.
The net force is zero due to repulsion between the Cooper pairs.
The superconductor excludes magnetic fields at very low temperatures.
Below the critical temperature a superconductor develops persistent screening currents that produce their own magnetic field.
Those currents respond to the field of the approaching magnet. Consider what they do to the magnetic flux that is trying to link with the superconductor, and hence to the force on the magnet.
D

When the material is cooled below its critical temperature it becomes a perfect diamagnet, the Meissner effect. Surface currents appear in the superconductor and generate a magnetic field that opposes the field of the nearby magnet, so magnetic flux is excluded from the bulk of the material. The upward force from this field balances the weight of the magnet, so the magnet hovers at a fixed height and never touches the surface.

The distractor statements all misidentify the mechanism. The levitating force is magnetic, arising from induced currents, so the option invoking electrostatic repulsion fails, and repulsion between Cooper pairs is not the origin of the force either. The field is not frozen into the material at low temperature, it is excluded from it, which rules out the freezing option. Only the statement that the superconductor excludes magnetic fields at very low temperatures describes the effect correctly.

content.text:
A block of silicon doped with boron is connected as shown in the diagram below.

What is the main way in which conduction occurs in the doped silicon block?

content.alt_text: A shaded silicon block connected in a single loop to a 10 V cell. The cell symbol has its long (positive) line on the left and short thick line on the right, so the block is connected to the positive terminal on its left.

content.text: Valence band electrons move to the right.
Valence band electrons move to the left.
Conduction band electrons move to the right.
Conduction band electrons move to the left.
Boron has one fewer valence electron than silicon, so each boron atom leaves a hole in the valence band. That makes the block a p-type semiconductor whose charge carriers are valence band electrons.
Electrons are attracted towards the positive terminal of the cell. Use the cell symbol to work out which side of the block that terminal is on.
B

Boron has three valence electrons while silicon has four. A boron atom substituted into the silicon lattice therefore forms one fewer bond than it needs, leaving a hole in the valence band, and the doped block is a p-type semiconductor.

In a p-type material the majority carriers are valence band electrons hopping into neighbouring holes, so conduction band electrons are not the main carriers. This eliminates the two options referring to conduction band electrons.

Electrons are negatively charged, so inside the block they drift towards the positive terminal of the cell. In the diagram the long (positive) line of the cell is on the left, so the block is joined to the positive terminal on its left and the valence band electrons move to the left. The leftward motion of the valence band electrons is therefore correct, matching the stored key.

content.text: Using a diagram and text, describe how an investigation can be performed to demonstrate the production and reception of radio waves.

An investigation of this kind needs a source that produces the waves and a detector that responds to them, with both working independently of any broadcast station. Think about which electrical discharge produces very high frequency oscillations.
A radio receiver works as the detector, but it must be tuned to a region of the spectrum where no station is broadcasting, so that any sound heard can only have come from the source.

Structure the description as a controlled test: state what the receiver does before the source is switched on, what changes when it is switched on, and label on the diagram which component produces the waves and which component detects them.

A valid set-up: a spark gap of about 5 mm connected to an induction coil and a DC power supply, placed near a hand-held radio tuned so that it does not receive a station. Switching on the power produces a spark across the gap, and the radio crackles with static.

The induction coil was set up and the radio tuned so it did not receive a station. Moving around the room and scanning the tuner across the range of wavelengths and frequencies located the position where the radio received static noise. When the power to the induction coil was switched on and a spark appeared across the gap, the radio crackled and made static noises. We inferred that the radio waves were produced by the induction coil and received by the radio.

content.text: From the graph, what is the gravitational potential energy of the mass when it is one Earth radius above Earth’s surface?
Move one Earth radius along the horizontal axis from the origin, then read across to the curve and down to the vertical axis.
Check the scale on the vertical axis before you record anything, since it is given in units of $10^{8}\,\mathrm{J}$ rather than in joules.

One Earth radius above the surface is the first labelled division on the horizontal axis. Reading across to the curve and then down to the vertical axis puts the potential energy at about $-0.7$ on a scale whose units are $10^{8}\,\mathrm{J}$.

The value is negative because the mass is still bound to the Earth at this height, and it is much less negative than the value at the surface, which is the trend the curve shows. The official 2008 HSC Physics marking guidelines give $-0.7 \times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{J}$ as the sample answer for this part.

content.text: Use an equation to explain why the graph is a curve and not a straight line.
Start from the two-body equation for gravitational potential energy and decide which quantity on the right-hand side is the one changing as the mass is raised.

content.text: “The work of scientists is influenced by external factors.”
Do you agree? Justify your answer with reference to the work of a scientist in the development of
Choose ONE of the following:

• space exploration
OR
• large-scale electricity distribution systems.
Choose ONE of the two areas and name the scientist or scientists you are writing about before you commit to an opinion. The knowledge of the work comes first in the marking scheme.
For the chosen area, list the external factors operating at the time: funding, government policy, military competition, commercial rivalry, or the demands of industry and the public.

Your justification must connect a specific external factor to a specific decision or direction taken by the scientist, and the whole argument has to read as one coherent piece rather than a list of factors.

Answers could include: “I would agree with this statement. The distribution of electricity was influenced by forces in society and in government. With the need for electrical energy to supply both population and industry increasing, scientists such as Edison and Westinghouse were pushed by offers of financial gain to direct their attention to lower cost, more efficient methods of producing and transporting electrical energy. Hence the competition between the Edison DC supply and the Westinghouse AC supply.” OR the equivalent response on von Braun and the V-2 rocket.

This is a choice-and-justify question, so a full response has to contain four things in a sensible order: a stated opinion, detailed knowledge of the work of the scientist or scientists chosen, identification of the external factors operating at the time, and an explicit justification that links each external factor to what the scientist actually did. External factors with no link to the work, or knowledge of the work with no external factors, cap the response well below the top band.

Working through the space exploration option. The external factors were the military competition of the Second World War, in which the V-2 was developed primarily as a weapon; the political pressure of the space race after 1957, when Soviet orbital successes galvanised government funding; and national prestige goals. The chain of reasoning runs: the V-2 was built under wartime secrecy and urgency, so von Braun's team worked to a military specification; after 1945 the same team transferred to work on the Redstone, Jupiter-C and finally the Saturn V vehicles, so the scale and direction of their work were set by defence and political imperatives rather than by the scientific problem alone. The opinion may then be expressed in either direction, provided it is argued from that evidence.

Working through the large-scale electricity distribution option. The external factors were the rapid growth in demand for electricity from both population and industry, the availability of the capital needed to build generating stations, and intense commercial rivalry. The reasoning runs: as the need for electrical energy to supply both population and industry increased, scientists and engineers such as Edison and Westinghouse were pushed by the offer of financial gain to direct their attention to lower cost and more efficient methods of producing and transporting electrical energy, and the competition between the Edison DC supply and the Westinghouse AC supply decided which system was developed further. The war of currents, the scale of the generating stations, and the emphasis on transmission efficiency are all traceable to those external pressures.

Weighing the two against the statement, the work in both areas is better described as directed and constrained by external factors than as independent of them: neither the V-2 and Saturn V programme nor the AC distribution system would have been attempted at that scale, or in that direction, without the military, political or commercial pressures identified. The opinion itself may be disagreement, provided the judgement is supported by specific, correctly recalled detail about the scientist's work.

content.text: Explain why the development of transformers was necessary to enable the large-scale distribution of electrical power.
Begin with where the energy is lost. Identify the expression that gives the power lost in a transmission line, and note the two quantities in it that a supply authority can actually control.

For a fixed power to be delivered, the expression $P = VI$ links the transmission voltage to the current, so work out what happens to $I$ — and therefore to the $I^{2}R$ loss — when the voltage is raised.

The word doing the work in the question is 'necessary', so finish by explaining why generating at the transmission voltage, or simply stepping the voltage down at the user's premises, is not a practical alternative, and why a local generator could not do the same job.

Power is lost in transmission lines ($P_{loss} = I^2R$). Stepping the voltage up before transmission reduces the current for the same power, so less energy is wasted, enabling supply over large distances.

Large-scale distribution of electrical power is difficult over long distances due to the large power losses, which occur in the transmission lines. This loss can be calculated from $P_{loss} = I^2R$. Transformers can be used to step up the voltage before transmission, so for example, if the transmission voltage is doubled, the current is halved and the power loss is reduced by a factor of four. This means that using transformers enables electrical energy to be supplied over large distances without wasting too much energy.

content.text: How did Einstein’s theory of special relativity and his explanation of the photoelectric effect lead to the reconceptualisation of the model of light?

Treat the two pieces of work separately at first, because each one attacks a different weakness of the wave model: one concerns the frame of reference, the other concerns how light interacts with matter.

For the photoelectric effect, begin with the observations classical theory could not explain — the threshold frequency, and the linear relationship between maximum kinetic energy and frequency — and then set out the photon model and the energy balance, including what the threshold represents.

For the reconceptualisation, be precise about what light was before and after in each case: a continuous wave that required a medium, compared with a wave that propagates itself, and a continuous wave compared with a stream of discrete quanta.

The photoelectric effect showed light behaves as photons ($E = hf = W + E_K$), reconceptualising light from a continuous wave into a stream of photons; special relativity showed the speed of light in vacuum is constant for all observers, reconceptualising light from something that needed a medium (the aether) into self-propagating electromagnetic waves.

The photoelectric effect refers to the release of an electron from the surface of a metal exposed to electromagnetic radiation. Classical physics was unable to explain the photoelectric effect, in particular the threshold frequency, which is the frequency of light at which electrons are emitted from the surface of a metal. It predicted that energy from light would be absorbed over time until an electron had sufficient energy to leave the surface of the metal. Einstein used Planck’s theory and the concept that photons carried energy to explain the photoelectric effect. Einstein assumed that light existed as photons, each with an energy equal to $E = hf$ and that the number of photons determined the light intensity. Photons with the highest energy correspond to the highest frequency, and an electron would not be emitted from a metal surface unless the photons possessed energy equal to or greater than the energy needed to overcome the energy holding the electron on the metal surface. The energy required to release the electron from the surface was called the work function, $W$. Einstein was able to combine the photon energy with the work function and the KE of the emitted electrons in the equation $E = hf = W + E_K$.

content.text: Both generators turn at the same rate, so both traces have the same period and the same peak magnitude — only the shape within one cycle differs.
Sketch first the generator whose brushes swap connections every half turn, and decide what that does to the sign of the voltage delivered to the external circuit.

Generator X: a train of positive pulses — the voltage never goes negative and returns to zero twice in every cycle (full-wave rectified DC). Generator Y: a sine wave that reverses polarity about zero each half cycle (AC). Both traces have the same period and the same peak magnitude, because the two machines rotate at the same rate.
Both machines contain the same coil turning at the same rate, so the emf induced in the coil is the same sinusoid, alternating in sign twice per revolution:

Generator X takes its output through a split-ring commutator. Every half turn the brushes swap to the other half of the coil, so whichever half-cycle is being induced is reconnected with the same sign. The output current therefore flows one way only: on the voltage-time graph that is a train of positive humps that touch zero twice per cycle, not a straight line.
Generator Y uses slip-rings, which do not swap connections, so the alternating emf reaches the external circuit unchanged: the trace is a sine wave about zero that reverses polarity every half cycle.

Equal rotation rates mean equal periods and equal peak magnitudes for the two traces; only the handling of the sign differs. Sketch the humps and the sine wave at the same peak height and with the same number of cycles over the same time axis.

content.text: Explain how the difference in connection to the external circuit accounts for the different output voltages.
Identify first which generator delivers current in one direction only and which reverses it, then explain why.
Link each answer to the named component: a split-ring commutator swaps the coil connections each half turn, while slip-rings do not.

Generator X is a DC generator using a split-ring commutator, so the brushes swap connections each half turn and the current flows in one direction only. Generator Y is an AC generator using slip-rings, so the current flows in both directions.

Generator X is a DC generator. The voltage is transferred to the external circuit via the brushes that make contact with the split-ring commutator. When the voltage of the coil changes direction, the brushes swap over the side of the coil they are connected to, which causes the voltage supplied to the external circuit to be in one direction only. Generator Y is an AC generator, in which the coil is connected to the outside circuit by slip-rings, which rotate with the coil. This means that the voltage varies sinusoidally with time, which results in an alternating current.

content.text: An induction coil is a type of transformer that allows a small voltage to be stepped up to a higher voltage. An induction coil consists of a primary coil wound around an iron core and a secondary coil. The secondary coil can be moved sideways so that different lengths of the iron core are within the secondary coil.

The photographs show an induction coil with the secondary coil in two different arrangements with the power supply turned off. At sufficiently high voltages a spark can be produced between the secondary coil electrodes.

content.alt_text: Photograph of an induction coil, Arrangement A: the secondary coil is mounted on the right-hand end of the core so the primary coil and iron core are completely inside it. Two electrode posts project upward from the coil.

Photograph of an induction coil, Arrangement B: the secondary coil is mounted on the right-hand end while the primary coil is mounted well to the left, outside the secondary coil, so only part of the iron core lies within the secondary coil. Two electrode posts project upward from the coil.

content.text: Part (a) asks which arrangement couples the two coils better; part (b) asks why that coupling sets the size of the induced voltage.
For (b) remember what a transformer relies on: the flux produced in the primary has to thread the secondary for a step-up voltage to appear.

items: 1 mark: part (a) identifies the correct photograph AND provides a reason
2 marks: part (b) shows how the effective turns ratio or magnetic coupling changes as the secondary coil is moved AND shows how the effective turns ratio changes …

content.text: Which arrangement would produce a spark when the power supply is turned on? Justify your choice.
Compare how much of the iron core, and how much of the primary coil, lies inside the secondary coil in each arrangement.
The spark needs the largest induced voltage, so ask which arrangement gives the better flux linkage.
Arrangement A, because the primary coil and iron core are completely inside the secondary coil.
A spark would be seen in photograph A because the primary coil and iron core are completely inside the secondary coil.

items: 1 mark: identifies the correct photograph AND provides a reason.

content.text: Explain how different voltages are induced when the secondary coil is moved to different positions.
Use the transformer relationship $V_p/V_s = N_p/N_s$ and remember that not every turn of the secondary is linked by the primary's flux.
Moving the secondary changes the fraction of the secondary that is linked, so the effective turns ratio and the induced voltage change together.
Moving the secondary coil changes the amount of flux that threads it, so a different voltage is induced.

Different voltages are produced when the secondary coil is moved to different positions, because of the amount of flux that threads the secondary coil. Transformers are designed so that almost all the magnetic flux produced in the primary coil threads the secondary coil, so that when an alternating current flows through the primary coil, a secondary magnetic flux passes through the secondary coil, thus producing an AC voltage at the terminals of the secondary coil. When the relative positions of the primary and secondary coils change, different amounts of flux thread the secondary coil and so a different voltage is produced.

content.text: You do not need to calculate anything for this part. The axes are already drawn with current on the vertical axis and potential difference on the horizontal one, so plot the wire $Y$ current values against the voltage values from the table, using the existing scale, and keep the plot points small and the trend line thin.

Before you draw the line, look at whether the ratio of current to voltage is the same for every wire $Y$ reading. If it is, the correct trend line is straight, and drawing a curve would lose the mark.

Then compare the two lines without stating your conclusion yet: at any given potential difference, is the wire $Y$ current above or below the wire $X$ line, and does the new line pass through the origin? Those two judgements are the whole of what the graph has to show.
Wire Y plots as a straight line of greater gradient than wire X (larger current for the same potential difference), passing through the origin.

The six wire $Y$ pairs to plot are $(0, 0)$, $(1.5, 0.20)$, $(3.0, 0.39)$, $(4.5, 0.59)$, $(6.0, 0.79)$ and $(7.5, 0.99)$ A against V. Using the printed axis ranges of 0 to 10 V horizontally and 0 to 3 A vertically, the last of these points sits at three quarters of the way along and at about one third of the current range.

The gradient implied by the data is constant: $0.20/1.5 = 0.133$, $0.39/3.0 = 0.130$, $0.59/4.5 = 0.131$, $0.79/6.0 = 0.132$ and $0.99/7.5 = 0.132\,\mathrm{A\,V^{-1}}$. Because that ratio does not drift, the correct trend line is a straight line through the origin of gradient about $0.13\,\mathrm{A\,V^{-1}}$, and all five non-zero points fall on it.

The wire $X$ line already on the graph has a gradient of about $0.38\,\mathrm{A\,V^{-1}}$, roughly three times greater, so the wire $Y$ line is much less steep and lies below the wire $X$ line everywhere except at the origin, where both pass through zero. Since a shallower gradient on a current-against-voltage graph means a larger resistance, wire $Y$ has about $1/0.132 = 7.6\,\Omega$ against $2.6\,\Omega$ for wire $X$, which is what part (b) asks you to confirm arithmetically. The marking guideline awards 2 marks for plotting the majority of points correctly and drawing a trend line that reflects them, and 1 mark for either on its own, so both the points and the line must be present.

content.text: Calculate the resistance of wire $Y$.

You want the resistance of the wire $Y$ itself, and the voltmeter is connected across the wire sample, so the tabulated potential difference is already the voltage across the wire. The 2 $\Omega$ series resistor is only there to protect the sample and needs no correction.

Use $R = V/I$ and take both values from the same row of the wire $Y$ columns. Using the row with the largest voltage gives the smallest percentage uncertainty, since the meter readings are most significant there.
Quote the answer to two significant figures and add the unit, and check that it is of the same order as the reciprocal of the gradient of the line you drew in part (a).
$R = 7.6\,\Omega$
$R = V/I = 7.5\,\mathrm{V}/0.99\,\mathrm{A} = 7.6\,\Omega$

items: 1 mark: identifies the correct formula and substitutes correctly.

content.text: Which sample of wire was pure chromium? Justify your response with reference to your graph.

Turn the question into a resistance comparison first. On a graph of current against potential difference the gradient is $1/R$, so the line that is steeper is the wire with the smaller resistance. Decide that from the graph, since the guideline requires the choice to be justified by reference to the graph.

Only then give the physical reason, and make it about scattering rather than about the wires looking different. Think about what happens to the regular arrangement of lattice ions when a second metal is dissolved into chromium to make nichrome, and what that does to the motion of the conduction electrons.
A two-mark answer needs both halves: the resistance comparison, and the pure-metal-versus-alloy argument that turns it into an identification of which sample was pure chromium.
Wire X was pure chromium ($R = 6.0/2.28 = 2.63\,\Omega$), because a pure metal has lower resistance than an alloy.

The resistance of wire X is $R = 6.0\,\mathrm{V}/2.28\,\mathrm{A} = 2.63\,\Omega$. The resistance of a pure metal is less than an alloy because of reduced electron scattering. Therefore, wire X is the pure chromium wire and wire Y is the nichrome wire.

items: 2 marks: correctly identifies that the resistance of wire X is less than that of wire Y AND supports the choice with reference to the graph.
1 mark: either of the above.

content.text: When the data for wire $X$ was plotted, one data point was considered inconsistent and was disregarded when drawing the trend line for calculating its resistance.
Suggest a physical reason why this data point is inconsistent with the trend line.

Read the outlier against the trend line before you explain anything. The point at $7.5\,\mathrm{V}$ falls below the wire $X$ line, so at that voltage the current is smaller than the line predicts. Translate that into a statement about the resistance of the sample at that moment.

Now ask why the resistance of a metal would be larger for one reading than for the others. Look at what is different about this reading: it has the largest voltage and therefore the largest power dissipated in the sample. Where does that power go, and what does a hotter lattice do to the conduction electrons?
The mark scheme awards the single mark for any physical reason, but a restatement of the data scores nothing, so the explanation has to name a physical effect rather than a discrepancy.
The power dissipated at that applied voltage heated the sample, raising its resistance through enhanced electron scattering by atomic vibrations.

The inconsistent point is (7.5, 2.5). This is below the trend line for wire X, indicating that the resistance of the wire has increased. This is because the power dissipated by the sample at this applied voltage is sufficient to heat the sample, increasing its resistance through enhanced electron scattering by atomic vibrations.

items: 1 mark: puts forward a physical reason.

content.text: Geophysics

This module question runs from a classification table to wave models to satellite images to instrumentation, and the four parts are independent, so do not let an idea from one part leak into another. Part (a) is reading a table, part (b) is reading two wave diagrams and comparing them, part (c) is comparing two images of the same scene, and part (d) is a comparison of two instruments.

In part (b) the horizontal scale under each diagram is 1 cm = 1 km and the snapshots are one second apart, so both speeds come from a distance on the scale divided by 1 s. Read the pulse positions carefully, and remember that the speed of a wave is the speed of the disturbance, not the speed of the medium.

Part (b)(ii) is worth 4 marks and is about what happens when a seismic wave meets a boundary between two different materials. Have the two terms ready: reflection, where part of the wave is sent back, and refraction, where the wave changes direction because its speed changes. Then attach each to $S$ and $P$ waves, which differ because one is transverse and the other longitudinal.

Part (d) is a comparison, so use the same headings for each instrument: structure, function, and what the information it gives about the Earth's interior. The third heading is where the marks are concentrated, so do not stop at describing the devices.

content.text: Part (a)(i) is three single-word answers, one for each blank, so read the two columns that are given and ask what a method based on that property is actually used to find. The property column tells you what the method responds to, and the application column tells you what has to be found in the ground.

Be careful with the third row: the property given is the elasticity of the medium, so the application is the one that uses the arrival of the waves from a distant event rather than a survey of a local one.

Part (a)(ii) is worth 3 marks and the mark scheme wants three separate things, so structure the answer as a list: the information the method produces, the picture of the Earth it supports, and the link between them. Choosing one method and doing it thoroughly scores more than naming all four.

items: (i) $X$ = locating ore bodies, mineral deposits, groundwater, oil or natural gas. $Y$ = electrical resistance (equivalently, conductivity). $Z$ = the study of earthquakes, that is locating epicentres and investigating the Earth's interior.

(ii) Using the seismic method: the information is in the travel times and speeds of the $P$ and $S$ waves, together with the directions in which they return. Because wave speed depends on the elasticity and density of the material, and because a wave is reflected and refracted wherever those properties change, the recorded travel times give the number of layers in the Earth, the depth of each boundary and the material of each layer, which allows models of the Earth to be constructed, tested and revised.

content.text: (a)(i) The gravitational method responds to differences in density. Surfaces of equal density are not perfectly smooth, and the instrument measures those variations, so it is used to locate buried bodies whose density differs from the surrounding rock: ore bodies and mineral deposits, the water table and groundwater, and accumulations of oil and natural gas. Any of those earns the mark for $X$. The electrical method responds to how easily a current passes through the ground, so the missing property is resistance, or equivalently conductivity; the presence of water in pore space lowers the resistance of rock dramatically, which is why the method is used to find water. The seismic method responds to the elasticity of the medium, and the application listed as $Z$ is the study of earthquakes, because a seismometer at the surface records the $P$ and $S$ waves from a distant epicentre and the arrival times locate it and probe the interior.

(a)(ii) The guideline asks for the type of information generated, an understanding of the Earth, and the link between them, so all three must be explicit. The seismic method is the best choice. The information is the set of travel times, speeds, amplitudes and directions of the returned waves. The understanding of the Earth is a stratified model with known number of layers, known depths and known compositions. The link is causal: the speed of a seismic wave is set by the elasticity and density of the medium it is in, so a wave changes speed and direction, and is partly reflected, whenever it crosses a boundary; measuring how long the direct and reflected waves take therefore gives the depth of each boundary, and the fact that the speeds change by particular amounts identifies what each layer is made of. Because a good model must account for all the observations, repeated surveys of this kind have been used to construct, test and discard models of the Earth's interior, and that is what has produced the accepted layered picture with a liquid outer core.

A horizontal scale marked 0 to 7 with 1 cm = 1 km is shown below. From t = 0 s to t = 1 s the pulse moves from about 0.6 km to about 2.2 km.

content.text: A $P$ wave can be modelled by a compression wave sent along a slinky spring as indicated below.

content.alt_text: Three snapshots of a compression wave travelling along a slinky spring, labelled t = 0 s, t = 1 s and t = 2 s, with the region of close coils moving from left to right. A horizontal scale marked 0 to 7 with 1 cm = 1 km is shown below.

content.text: Both diagrams use the same scale, 1 cm = 1 km, and both show the wave at $t = 0$, $1$ and $2$ s, so each speed is a distance read off the scale divided by 1 s. Read the position of the crest for the string and the position of the region of closest coils for the slinky, and subtract the $t = 0$ position from the $t = 1$ s position rather than reading an absolute position.

For the second half, remember that a seismic wave is a mechanical wave, so every statement about the string and the slinky transfers to rock. The words to define carefully are reflection, where part of the wave is sent back into the medium it came from, and refraction, where the wave changes direction because its speed has changed at the boundary.

Then attach the physics to the two wave types. The $S$ wave is transverse and needs a medium with rigidity, so it is the slower of the pair; the $P$ wave is longitudinal and compressional, and is faster. Because the two speeds differ so much they are refracted by very different amounts at the same boundary, which is the reason earthquakes can be located from the gap between their arrivals.

items: (ii) At any interface where the elasticity or density of the medium changes, for example where soil meets rock, a proportion of the wave is reflected back into the first medium and the remainder is transmitted into the second. The transmitted wave is refracted, that is bent, because its speed changes at the boundary; it bends towards the normal when it slows down. Both $S$ and $P$ waves are reflected and refracted in this way. The $S$ wave is transverse, needs a rigid medium, cannot pass through a liquid, and is much the slower, so it is refracted far more strongly. The $P$ wave is longitudinal and compressional, is faster, and can travel through both solids and liquids.

content.text: (i) The horizontal scale below each diagram is marked 1 cm = 1 km and the snapshots are one second apart, so the calculation is the same for both. For the string the crest of the transverse pulse is at about 0.6 km at $t = 0\,\mathrm{s}$ and about 2.2 km at $t = 1\,\mathrm{s}$, giving a displacement of 1.6 km in 1 s.
For the slinky the closely packed coils, which mark the compression, are at about 1.0 km at $t = 0\,\mathrm{s}$ and about 3.0 km at $t = 1\,\mathrm{s}$, giving 2.0 km in 1 s.

The guideline awards one mark for converting the scale readings to kilometres and one mark for each correctly substituted speed, so the subtraction and the division must both be shown. The transverse disturbance on the string models the $S$ wave and the compression on the slinky models the $P$ wave, and the model reproduces the real ordering: the $P$ wave is the faster. Note that what is being measured is the speed of the pattern through the medium, not the speed of the medium, since neither the string nor the coils travel from $t = 0$ to $t = 1$ s.

(ii) Two marks are for the physics of the interface and two for relating it to the two wave types. When a seismic wave reaches a boundary at which the elasticity or density changes, the wave cannot carry on in the same way, so it splits: a part is reflected back into the medium it came from, with the angle of reflection equal to the angle of incidence, and a part is transmitted into the new medium. The transmitted part is refracted, because its speed in the new medium is different, and it bends towards the normal when it enters a slower medium. The reflection is what a geophone or seismometer at the surface records, and its delay is how the depth of the boundary is found. Both $S$ and $P$ waves behave this way at the same boundaries, but they differ in the details that matter. The $S$ wave is transverse, so its restoring force is the shear rigidity of the medium; it needs a medium that can resist shear, so it cannot propagate through a liquid, and its speed is highly sensitive to the rigidity, rising sharply as the material stiffens, which makes it the slower of the two, about $1.6\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ in the model and $3$ to $4\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ in real rock. The $P$ wave is longitudinal and compressional, is governed mainly by the bulk modulus, is faster, about $2.0\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ in the model and $6$ to $8\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ in real rock, and can pass through liquids. Because the two speeds differ by so much they are refracted by very different amounts, the $S$ wave being bent much more strongly, and this is the basis of earthquake location: the larger the gap between the $P$ and $S$ arrivals at a station, the further away the epicentre is.

It is worth adding that the $S$ wave's inability to pass through liquid is what identified the outer core of the Earth as liquid, and that the two facts together, refraction and the $S$-wave shadow zone, are among the strongest pieces of evidence for the layered structure of the planet.

content.text: The two images were taken at the same instant by the same satellite, so time and viewpoint are ruled out and the difference has to be a difference in the physics. For each image, identify the part of the electromagnetic spectrum the sensor used, and then ask what quantity of the surface that band actually measures.

For the visible image the measured quantity is reflected sunlight, so the shading is about how much each surface reflects. For the thermal image the measured quantity is the infrared radiation the surface emits, so the brightness is about temperature. Once you have that, the dark patches and the bright hot spots in each image explain themselves.

Part (c)(ii) has three separate marks, so write three separate points: a feature of the monitoring, what the technique lets authorities do, and the benefit that follows. Repeated wide-area coverage without needing to reach the site is the feature to lead with, because everything else depends on it.

items: (i) The visible image is produced from the visible part of the electromagnetic spectrum, so it records sunlight reflected by the surface. Smoke, sea, burnt ground and healthy vegetation all absorb and reflect different fractions of the incident light, so they appear with different shades, which is why the burnt forest reads as dark patches and the smoke plume stands out over the water. The thermal image is produced from the infrared part of the spectrum, so it records the thermal radiation emitted by the surface itself; the actively burning areas are at a much higher temperature than the surroundings, so they appear bright white and with far greater contrast than in the visible image. The satellite orbits above the region and its sensors record the data and transmit it to a ground station for processing.

(ii) Remote sensing gives repeated, large-area, timely coverage of a region without anyone having to reach it. That allows fires, floods, oil spills, drought, changes in vegetation and the movement of ice to be tracked while they are still developing, so a warning can be issued in time and aircraft, crews and equipment can be sent to the right place. The result is that lives, money and equipment are saved, which is both an economic and a social benefit.

content.text: (i) Three marks are available and the guideline asks for the band of the spectrum matched to the image and the technique, the role of differences in absorption and reflection, and the role of the satellite itself. The visible-light sensor works in the visible band and forms an image from sunlight that has been reflected off the surface. What reaches the sensor therefore depends on how much each surface reflects: sea water absorbs strongly and so appears dark, healthy vegetation reflects a good fraction of green light, burnt and charred ground absorbs much more than unburnt vegetation and so appears as dark patches, and the smoke plume scatters and absorbs light differently from the air behind it, which is why the plume is visible over the sea. The thermal-infrared sensor works in a much longer-wavelength band and forms its image from the infrared radiation the surface emits, whose intensity rises steeply with temperature. The regions where the fire is actually burning are at temperatures of hundreds of degrees Celsius while the surrounding land and sea are near ambient, so those regions appear bright white and stand out with a contrast the visible image cannot match. That contrast is why fire detection and fire-front mapping use the thermal band. The satellite itself is what makes the technique possible: it holds a stable position above the region or passes over it on a fixed cycle, its sensors collect the data with a range of detectors, and the data are transmitted back to Earth for processing and comparison with previous passes.

(ii) The guideline awards one mark for a feature of the monitoring, one for the role of the technique in management and control, and one for the benefits. Features of the monitoring: the coverage is very large in area, the data are collected repeatedly so they form a continuous record rather than a single snapshot, and they are available within hours, all without anyone having to reach the site, which for a wildfire or a flood is often impossible. Role in management and control: because the record is timely and repeated, the images can be used to follow an event as it develops and to predict where it is heading, so a warning can be issued to the communities in its path while there is still time to act, and emergency services, aircraft, ships and equipment can be directed to the affected area rather than deployed blindly. Benefits: this saves lives, money and resources, and it does so with both economic and social value, since the people saved are the same people whose homes and livelihoods would otherwise be lost. The same features are why remote sensing is used for climate monitoring, for tracking pollution and for mapping hazards such as floods, landslides and coastal erosion.

content.text: Both geophones and seismometers detect seismic activity.
Compare the structure and function of these devices and the information they provide about the large-scale structure of the Earth.

This is a comparison, so build the answer from the same three headings for each device: how it is put together, what it does, and what the data it produces reveal about the Earth's interior. Using parallel headings for the two instruments is what turns a list into a comparison and picks up the coherence mark.

For structure, think about what is actually moving in each instrument. In one case a coil is forced to move relative to a fixed magnet by the ground, which generates a current; in the other case a heavy mass stays still by inertia while the ground moves under it, and that relative motion is written to a rotating surface. That difference in mechanism is the whole of the structure contrast.

For the third heading, do not stop at 'they detect earthquakes'. The question asks what the information tells you about the large-scale structure of the Earth, and the key facts are that the two wave types travel at different speeds and that one of them cannot pass through a liquid. Work out what those two facts alone prove about the core.

Geophones set out in lines detect an induced current and provide a picture and depths of the subsurface. Seismometers detect vibrations on a revolving drum and give intensity in the horizontal and vertical directions; the P and S waves give evidence for the inner and outer core.

content.text: The transducer of an ultrasound machine.

Part (a) is one crystal doing two opposite jobs, and the mark scheme wants both jobs. Ask what a piezoelectric crystal does when a potential difference is applied across it, and then ask what it does when pressure is applied to it. The answer to the second is the reverse of the answer to the first, and that reversal is the detection mechanism.

Be specific about the kind of potential difference. A steady d.c. voltage distorts the crystal once and produces nothing sustained, so the source has to alternate, and the frequency of that alternation is the frequency of the emitted ultrasound.

For part (a)(ii) the key word is impedance, not intensity or density on its own. Define acoustic impedance as the product of density and the speed of sound in the tissue, then use the difference in that product between two tissues to explain both why a reflection occurs and why some boundaries echo much more strongly than others.

items: (i) Both functions rest on the piezoelectric effect in a crystal such as PZT. An alternating potential difference across the crystal makes it change shape repeatedly at the frequency of the supply, and those repeated changes launch an ultrasound wave. When a returning wave presses on the crystal, the pressure deforms it and this generates a varying potential difference across it, which is the electrical signal the machine uses.

(ii) As the ultrasound travels through the body it crosses many interfaces between different tissues. At each one a proportion of the wave is reflected and the rest transmitted, and the amount reflected is set by the difference in acoustic impedance $Z$ between the two tissues, $Z$ being the product of tissue density and the speed of sound in it. A small difference in $Z$ gives a weak echo, while a large difference, such as soft tissue against bone or any boundary involving gas, gives a strong one. The transducer records the intensity and the delay of each echo, the delay giving the depth of the boundary and the intensity indicating the nature of the tissues meeting there.

content.text: (a)(i) The guideline awards three marks: identify the piezoelectric effect as the basis of production and of detection, and give the reason for each. A piezoelectric crystal is one that becomes mechanically deformed when placed in an electric field, and conversely develops a potential difference when it is deformed. For production, the crystal in the transducer is driven by an alternating potential difference, so its deformation is reversed at every half cycle; each reversal pushes on the surrounding fluid and launches a wave, and because the driving frequency is in the megahertz range the wave is ultrasound. A steady d.c. voltage would distort the crystal once and produce no sustained wave, which is why the excitation must alternate. For detection, a returning ultrasound wave exerts a varying pressure on the same crystal; that pressure deforms it, and by the converse of the piezoelectric effect the deformation generates a varying potential difference across the crystal, with a magnitude proportional to the pressure and hence to the intensity of the echo. That alternating voltage is the signal the machine amplifies and displays. Using the same crystal for both jobs means one small component both produces and receives the beam, and allows the echo delay to be timed from a single point in the body.

(a)(ii) Ultrasound is a mechanical wave, so it needs a medium, and the body is a medium made of many tissues with different properties. As the wave travels it meets a boundary at almost every depth, and at each boundary the wave splits: part is reflected back into the tissue it came from and part is transmitted onwards into the next tissue, with a little energy absorbed. The proportion reflected is governed by the acoustic impedance of the tissues, defined as the product of the density of the tissue and the speed of sound in it. When the impedance changes abruptly, part of the wave cannot continue smoothly into the new medium and is sent back. The larger the difference in impedance between the two tissues, the greater the fraction of the wave reflected, so a boundary between two soft tissues of similar impedance returns a weak echo while a boundary between soft tissue and bone, or any boundary involving air or gas in the lung or bowel, returns a very strong one. Two consequences make the image possible. First, the different tissues give echoes of different intensities, so the returning signal carries information about which tissues are present and where their boundaries lie. Second, the time taken for an echo to return is proportional to the total distance travelled, and the speed of sound in tissue is nearly constant, so the delay converts directly into depth. The transducer therefore measures the intensity and the time of return of every echo and the machine builds the image from the complete set of echoes.

content.text: Endoscopy.

Part (b)(i) is only 2 marks but each use must be sketched in general terms, so give a purpose and a consequence for each, not just a name. One use is about seeing and one is about obtaining material, and choosing two uses from different categories is safer than two versions of the same idea.

Part (b)(ii) is worth 3 marks and the guideline is explicit that diagrams are part of the answer. Draw each bundle in cross-section, shade in a single fibre and trace a ray from one end to the other. The test is where the ray emerges: in one case it must emerge from the same end position it entered, and in the other it must not. That single difference is the physics and the roles follow from it.

Part (b)(iii) is a single mark for one advantage over alternative surgical procedures. Think about the size of the incision and the consequences of a large one, and about what the patient has to undergo. One clear advantage stated well is all that is needed.

items: (i) To view the internal structure of the body directly and so detect abnormality without having to open the body, and to take a sample of tissue for investigation from an area that is difficult to reach by any other means.

(ii) A coherent bundle keeps each fibre fixed in its position relative to the others along the whole length, so a ray entering one fibre leaves the bundle from the same end of that same fibre; drawn in cross-section the ray runs straight through one fibre. Its role is to carry a faithful image of the object being examined. An incoherent bundle has its fibres free to shuffle relative to one another, so a ray entering one fibre leaves from a different position entirely; drawn in cross-section the ray crosses repeatedly from fibre to fibre. Its role is to distribute light evenly and so illuminate the object being viewed. An endoscope contains both.

(iii) Endoscopy is minimally invasive compared with the surgery that would be needed to reach and open the same area, so the patient avoids a large incision, the associated blood loss and risk of infection, and in many cases general anaesthesia and a long recovery.

content.text: (b)(i) Two marks, one per use, and the guideline asks for them in general terms rather than as bare labels. The first use is diagnosis by direct observation: the endoscope carries light into a body cavity and returns an image of the lining, so the surgeon can see ulcers, inflammation, tumours or bleeding directly, at a resolution no external scan matches, and can make a diagnosis without opening the body. The second use is tissue sampling: a channel through the same instrument allows a small biopsy to be taken from a deep or awkward site, such as the lining of the stomach or the lung, for later examination in the laboratory, where the alternative would be a major operation purely to obtain the sample. Naming the two uses without describing them earns 1 mark; describing each in general terms earns the 2.

(b)(ii) Three marks, and the guideline requires both the differences and the roles, with the diagrams counting. The difference between the two bundles is whether the fibres are fixed in position relative to one another along their length. In a coherent bundle every fibre is rigidly fixed, so if you can see the end of the bundle and trace a particular fibre, you can follow it all the way; a ray entering at one end of a fibre therefore leaves from the same end of that same fibre. Drawn as a cross-section, the fibre positions are identical at both ends and the ray runs through one fibre without crossing. The consequence is that the spatial pattern of the light is preserved, so a coherent bundle transports an image faithfully, and its role in an endoscope is to return the image of the internal structure being examined to the eyepiece. In an incoherent bundle the fibres are not fixed; they are free to move relative to one another and are usually deliberately shuffled along their length, so a ray entering one fibre will emerge from an entirely different part of the end of the bundle. Drawn as a cross-section, the fibres at the two ends are not in the same order and the ray crosses from fibre to fibre repeatedly on its way along. The consequence is that light leaving any part of the end illuminates the whole of the other end, so the bundle's role is to deliver an even, shadow-free illumination of the object being viewed rather than to form an image. A real endoscope therefore contains two separate bundles, one of each type, for exactly these two reasons.

(b)(iii) One mark, and any well-stated advantage is accepted. The expected one is minimal invasiveness: reaching the same area surgically would require a large incision through skin, muscle and often bone, with the attendant blood loss, risk of infection, damage to adjacent structures and a long painful recovery, whereas the endoscope needs only a small opening and, in many cases, only local anaesthesia. Other acceptable points are that the operator sees the actual site rather than inferring it from an external image, and that investigation and treatment can be carried out during the one procedure.

content.text: Medical imaging of bone.

Part (c)(i) is a contrast, so the mark scheme will not give credit for two descriptions of the same technique. State the advantage of each in one sentence and then state explicitly how the advantages differ, because the guideline asks for that link.

For part (c)(ii) remember the whole chain: electrons must first be given very high speeds, then made to strike a target. Ask what happens to an electron when it is stopped abruptly, and ask separately what happens when it knocks an inner-shell electron out of a target atom.

Part (c)(iii) is about the substance, not the scan. For any candidate isotope ask three questions: does it emit the radiation the scanner detects, will it end up in the bone, and will it decay fast enough that the patient is not still carrying the dose after the scan is finished?

items: (i) X-ray images are quick and cheap to produce and show the structure and density of bone superbly, so they are the ideal first test for a fracture, a dislocation or a structural change in bone. Bone scans take hours, cost more and involve an injection, but they image the function and blood supply of the bone rather than its structure, so they detect abnormality before any structural change is visible, which widens the treatment options available and improves the success rate. The advantages therefore differ: X-rays are superior for structure and speed, bone scans for function and early detection.

(ii) Electrons are emitted from a heated cathode and accelerated across a high potential difference, of order 100 000 V, to very high velocities, then made to strike a target of tungsten. Some X-rays are produced by the rapid deceleration of the electrons as they are stopped in the target; others by the electrons colliding with and ejecting K-shell electrons from the tungsten atoms, after which higher-shell electrons drop into the vacancies and emit X-ray photons of energy equal to the difference between the shell energies.

(iii) The radiopharmaceutical must emit gamma radiation, because that is what the gamma camera detects. It must be taken up by and accumulate in the bone being examined, otherwise the image carries no anatomical information. Its half-life must be long enough for the scan to be completed but short enough that most of the dose has decayed away before the patient leaves, so the exposure adds negligible risk.

content.text: (c)(i) Three marks, and the guideline is explicit that both techniques must be discussed and that how their advantages differ must be made clear. X-ray imaging of bone has three practical advantages. It is quick, needing only a fraction of a second of exposure, and relatively cheap, so it can be used as a first-line test. It gives excellent contrast between tissues of different density, so the structure, alignment and density of bone are shown in fine detail. It is therefore ideal for detecting fractures, dislocations, and bone tumours that have already altered the structure, and for checking the setting of a bone. A bone scan has a quite different set of advantages. The tracer is injected, is carried by the blood and is taken up only where bone is active, so the scan maps the blood supply and the metabolic activity of the bone rather than its shape. It therefore shows abnormality early, including infection, inflammation and the early stages of tumours, at a stage when an X-ray is still normal, and the extra information guides treatment and gives an earlier diagnosis, which widens the treatment options and improves the success rate. The contrast to state explicitly is therefore: X-rays image structure quickly and cheaply and are the right choice for acute injury, whereas bone scans image function slowly and expensively and are the right choice for disease that has not yet distorted the bone.

(c)(ii) Two marks for features and characteristics, one for an outline, so the mechanism has to be given. X-rays are high-energy electromagnetic radiation, produced in an electron tube in two ways, and in both the electrons must first be given very high velocities and then made to strike a target. Electrons are released from a heated cathode and accelerated across a very high potential difference, of order 100 000 V, which gives them the required energy; they are then brought to rest abruptly by a target, usually tungsten because of its high melting point. In the first process, bremsstrahlung, an electron is decelerated in the Coulomb field of a target nucleus and radiates away its lost kinetic energy as an X-ray photon, giving a continuous spread of photon energies up to the full accelerating energy. In the second process, characteristic radiation, an incoming electron strikes a tungsten atom hard enough to eject a K-shell electron, leaving a vacancy; a higher-shell electron then drops into the vacancy and, because each shell has a fixed energy, the energy difference is emitted as a single X-ray photon, so sharp spectral peaks appear at the characteristic energies of tungsten. A third requirement to mention is that almost all of the electron energy becomes heat in the target, which is why the target is tungsten and is water-cooled. The quantity of X-rays produced is set by the tube current and the maximum photon energy by the accelerating voltage.

(c)(iii) Two marks, awarded for at least two suitable properties with their consequences, so three or four properties are the safe target. The radiation type: the gamma camera detects gamma rays, so a bone-scanning radiopharmaceutical must be a gamma emitter; a substance emitting only alpha or beta particles would give no useful external signal, because alpha and beta are absorbed in the body and cannot escape. Targeting and accumulation: the substance must be taken up by, and concentrate in, the bone or the organ under investigation, which is achieved by chemically attaching it to a molecule such as a phosphate ion that hydroxyapatite incorporates as new bone is laid down; without this the tracer would be spread through the blood and the image would be a featureless background rather than a picture of the skeleton. Half-life: it must be long enough that the patient can be injected, the tracer can distribute through the body and reach the bone, and the scan, which takes hours, can be completed, and short enough that the great majority of the dose has decayed away by the time the patient leaves, so no significant additional health risk is incurred. A fourth property sometimes credited is that the emitted photons should have an energy the gamma camera's collimator and detector can use efficiently, since very low energy photons are absorbed in the patient's own tissue before escaping and very high energy ones pass through the detector rather than being absorbed in the crystal. A fifth is that the substance should be chemically stable and of high radiochemical purity so that it remains in the intended form until it decays in the body.
