content.text: Explain how different medical imaging techniques use tomography to improve our diagnostic abilities.

Build this answer in two halves: the idea of tomography itself, and then the same idea applied to at least two named scans. The mark scheme awards the top band only when the concept, two applications and the effect on diagnosis are all present, so do not spend the whole answer on only one technique.

Define tomography in terms of slices and voxels: the body is cut into thin cross-sections, each section is divided into very small boxes called voxels, and one measurement is made on each voxel. Ask why that matters for diagnosis, and the answer involves detail and the ability to view the same data from many angles.

For the applications, the question is always 'what is actually measured in each voxel?'. For CT think absorption of X-rays; for MRI think the radio signal from hydrogen nuclei after nuclear magnetic resonance; for PET think the gamma rays from positron-electron annihilation. Two fully developed scans carry the top band.

Tomography slices the body into thin sections divided into voxels, with a measurement made for each voxel and the information rearranged to give views from many angles. CT uses X-ray absorption, MRI the radio signal from NMR and PET gamma emission from positron–electron annihilation, improving diagnostic detail and the detection of abnormality.

Tomography is a technique in which the body is “sliced” into thin sections and information from each section can be analysed to detect abnormalities. Each slice is further divided into voxels and some measurement is made regarding each voxel. This requires powerful computers to process, manage and present huge amounts of information. Since the voxels are so small, we can generally obtain good detail in the images. We can also rearrange the information to obtain views from a range of different angles. This provides improved diagnostic abilities. The information being presented varies with the imaging technique. CT scans are based on the X-ray absorption of each voxel. MRI scans are based on the radio signal emitted by each voxel after an NMR process, which allows the H content of each voxel, and hence its water content, to be determined. PET scans are based on the gamma radiation emitted from each voxel when electrons in the body interact with positrons produced by certain radioisotopes.

content.text: Astrophysics

This module question moves from spectra, to a table of stellar measurements, to the H-R diagram, to how stellar masses are inferred indirectly, and the four parts are independent. Part (a) is about how spectra are produced and what they reveal, part (b) is arithmetic on the table, part (c) is stellar structure and nucleosynthesis, and part (d) is measurement in astronomy.

The two calculations in part (b) use a feature worth stating before you start: the magnitude scale is logarithmic and inverted, so a star with a lower magnitude is brighter, and each difference of one magnitude corresponds to a factor of $100^{1/5} \approx 2.51$ in intensity. Getting the sign of the difference the right way round is what makes the ratio come out greater than one.

For the distance in part (b)(ii) use the distance modulus relation $m - M = 5\log_{10}(d/10)$ with $d$ in parsecs, and substitute the apparent and absolute magnitudes of the same star from the same row. The colour index in (b)(iii) is a difference of two magnitudes measured through different filters, so think about which filter each kind of star is relatively brighter through.

Part (c)(ii) requires you to use the H-R diagram, so identify where $X$ and $Y$ actually sit before writing: one of them is on the main sequence and the other is not. Then the reaction in each position follows from the stage of evolution that position represents. Part (c)(iii) is a flowchart, so a sequence with branches and outcomes is required, not a list.

content.text: The analysis of electromagnetic radiation is widely used by astronomers.

Part (a)(i) is about the two processes, not about the appearance of the two spectra, and the mark scheme wants the appearance as the outcome rather than the cause. For each, identify what is happening to the electrons: in one case they are falling and radiating, in the other they are being raised and then re-radiating at the same frequencies.

Once the processes are described, the comparison falls out: the emission spectrum has bright lines on a dark background and the absorption spectrum has dark lines on a continuous background, at exactly the same set of frequencies for the same element, because both are fixed by the same differences between energy levels.

Part (a)(ii) is worth 3 marks, so give two or more characteristics of stars and their motion and say what each reveals. Three areas cover the marks: what the star is made of, how hot its surface is, and how fast it is moving through space.

items: (i) An emission spectrum is produced when a substance is excited and then emits, with electrons dropping from higher to lower energy levels and radiating photons of exactly the energy difference between the levels, so bright lines appear at a few discrete frequencies on a dark background. An absorption spectrum is produced when a continuous beam of white light passes through the substance in its gaseous form, with electrons absorbing exactly the photons that match a level difference and being promoted, so those frequencies are missing from the transmitted light and dark lines appear on a continuous background. The line frequencies are the same in both, because both are set by the same differences between the atom's energy levels.

(ii) Spectroscopy reveals the elements present in the outer layers of the star and their relative abundances, from the identity and strength of the absorption lines. It reveals the surface temperature, because the temperature sets the distribution of electrons among the energy levels and so determines which transitions, and hence which lines, can occur. It reveals the motion of the star through space, because the Doppler effect displaces the whole pattern of lines to longer wavelengths when the star recedes and to shorter wavelengths when it approaches, and the size of that displacement gives the radial velocity.

content.text: (a)(i) The guideline awards 3 marks for showing how the production of the two spectra differs, 2 for outlining both, and 1 for either alone. An emission spectrum is obtained by exciting a substance, either by heating it or by passing a current through it at low pressure, so that its electrons are promoted to higher energy levels. When those electrons fall back to lower levels they emit photons, and because the difference in energy between two particular levels is a single fixed value, each allowed transition produces light of one definite frequency. Only those frequencies are present, so the spectrum appears as a set of coloured lines on a dark background, and the pattern of lines is a fingerprint of the element. An absorption spectrum is obtained differently. A continuous source, such as an incandescent lamp, is shone through the substance in its gaseous form. Photons whose energy happens to match a difference between the atom's energy levels are absorbed by the electrons, which are promoted to those levels, and those photons never emerge on the far side. Everything else is transmitted, so the result is a continuous spectrum interrupted by dark lines at the missing frequencies. The essential contrast is therefore emission versus absorption of the same quanta, and the essential similarity is that the frequencies involved are identical in the two spectra because they are fixed by the same set of energy levels, which is why an absorption spectrum looks like a photographic negative of the emission spectrum of the same element.

(a)(ii) The guideline awards 3 marks for features and characteristics of two relevant properties of stars and their motion, 2 for one characteristic with a description or two outlined, and 1 for a single characteristic. Composition: the light reaching Earth from a star has passed through its outer layers, so the absorption lines in its spectrum are produced by the atoms of those layers. Each element has its own set of line frequencies, so identifying the lines identifies the elements present, and the strength and number of lines belonging to each element indicate its relative abundance. This is how the hydrogen and helium dominance of ordinary stars and the presence of heavier elements in some stars were established. Surface temperature: a star's spectrum is formed in its photosphere, and the temperature there sets the distribution of electrons among the atomic energy levels according to Boltzmann statistics, so hot stars show transitions from high levels and cool stars transitions from low levels, and the pattern of lines present therefore reveals the surface temperature, which is what defines the spectral classes O to M on the H-R diagram. Motion: the frequencies emitted by a star are altered on the way to Earth by the Doppler effect, so the entire pattern of lines is shifted to longer wavelengths for a receding star and to shorter wavelengths for an approaching one. Measuring that shift gives the component of the star's velocity along the line of sight, and the same effect applied to whole galaxies is the primary evidence that the universe is expanding. Rotation can also be detected, by the broadening and asymmetry of the lines.

content.text: Before calculating anything, state the property of the magnitude scale you need: it is logarithmic and inverted, so a star of lower apparent magnitude is brighter, and a difference of one magnitude is a factor of about 2.51 in intensity. Writing that down first prevents a sign error in part (i).

Part (b)(i) compares two stars as seen from Earth, so only apparent magnitudes are involved and the distance of each star cancels out. Form the difference in the right order, brightest minus faintest, so the exponent comes out positive.

Part (b)(ii) is a different relation altogether. Use the distance modulus $m - M = 5\log_{10}(d/10)$ with $d$ in parsecs, take $m$ and $M$ from the same row of the table, and check your answer by asking whether the star is intrinsically brighter or fainter than it appears; a star that is much more luminous than it looks must be far away.

Part (b)(iii) is about the filters, not about the star. $B$ and $V$ are magnitudes measured through a blue and a yellow-green filter, and because the scale is inverted a star that is relatively brighter in one filter has the lower magnitude there. Work out which filter each kind of star favours and the sign of the difference follows.

items: (i) Sirius A appears $17.5$ times brighter than Bellatrix, because $100^{(1.64 - (-1.47))/5} = 17.5$.
(ii) Regulus A is about $24\,\mathrm{pc}$ away, roughly $7.3\times10^{17}\ \mathrm{m}$, from $1.35 - (-0.52) = 5\log_{10}(d/10)$.

(iii) The colour index is $\mathrm{CI} = B - V$. A cool star radiates most of its energy at the red end, so it is relatively brighter through the yellow-green $V$ filter than through the blue $B$ filter; because the magnitude scale is inverted, its $V$ magnitude is the more negative, so $B - V$ is positive. A hot star radiates most of its energy in the blue, is relatively brighter through $B$, and so has a negative colour index.

content.text: (b)(i) Two marks, for the correct formula and correct substitution. Sirius A has an apparent magnitude of $-1.47$ and Bellatrix $+1.64$, so the difference in magnitude between them is
Because the magnitude scale is logarithmic and inverted, a difference $\Delta m$ corresponds to a ratio of intensities of $100^{\Delta m/5}$.

Sirius A is therefore 17.5 times brighter to an eye at Earth. Note the two traps. The subtraction must be faintest minus brightest, that is $1.64 - (-1.47)$ and not the reverse, or the ratio comes out as a fraction. And the conversion is $100^{\Delta m/5}$, which is $10^{\Delta m/2.5}$; reading $100^{0.622}$ as $4.2$ is an arithmetic slip, since $100^{0.622} = 10^{2\times 0.622} = 10^{1.244} = 17.5$. Only apparent magnitudes are used, which is correct, because the question asks about the appearance from Earth and the distances of the two stars therefore cancel out of the ratio. The official 2008 guideline gives 17.5, which agrees.

(b)(ii) Two marks, for correct substitution including units. Absolute magnitude is defined as the apparent magnitude a star would have at a distance of 10 parsecs, so apparent magnitude, absolute magnitude and distance are related by the distance modulus.

Regulus A is at about 24 parsecs, which is $23.7 \times 3.086\times10^{16} = 7.3\times10^{17}\,\mathrm{m}$. The check on the sign is informative: Regulus A has a positive apparent magnitude but a more negative absolute magnitude, so it is intrinsically far more luminous than it appears and must therefore be far away, which is what the positive result confirms. Taking the magnitudes the other way round would give a negative logarithm and an impossible negative distance. Note that the official 2008 marking guideline prints 24.7 pc for this part; that figure is not consistent with the magnitudes printed in the paper and with the formula the guideline itself quotes, both of which give 23.7 pc, so 24 pc is quoted here and the discrepancy is flagged in the notes on the parent question.

(b)(iii) Three marks, for the determination of the colour index and for the reason cool stars have the more positive value. The colour index is defined as the difference between the star's photographic blue magnitude and its visual magnitude,

where $B$ is the magnitude measured through a blue filter and so measures the blue light the star emits, and $V$ is the magnitude measured through a yellow-green filter and so measures the yellow-green light it emits. A cooler star is towards the red end of the spectrum, so compared with a hot star it emits relatively less blue light and relatively more yellow-green light. It is therefore brighter through the $V$ filter, and because the magnitude scale is inverted, brightness means a lower, that is more negative, magnitude, so $V$ is more negative than $B$ and $B - V$ is a positive number. A hotter star is the reverse: it emits relatively more blue light, is brighter through the $B$ filter, has a more negative $B$, and so a negative colour index. The table shows the trend: Betelgeuse, a cool supergiant, has a colour index of $+1.85$, while Regulus A at $-0.11$ and Bellatrix at $-0.22$ are hotter stars with small negative values, and Sirius A at $+0.01$ is near zero because it is roughly balanced. The third mark in the guideline is for the reasoning that connects the filter response to the sign, not for restating the definition.

content.text: The HR diagram below shows positions X and Y.

Part (c)(i) is about the two competing processes in a forming star, one that compresses and one that expands, and the mark scheme wants each with the reason it occurs. Do not leave it at 'gravity pulls in and pressure pushes out'; say what the pressure is and where its energy comes from.

Part (c)(ii) is a reading of the H-R diagram, so begin by locating $X$ and $Y$. Ask in each case where the star is in its life: a star on the main sequence is still fusing hydrogen, and a star sitting above and to the cool side of the main sequence has already run out of hydrogen in its core. The reaction in each position then follows from that, and you must name the pathway, not just the fuel.

Part (c)(iii) asks for a flowchart, so draw boxes and arrows. A red giant has more than one possible end, so the chart has a branch, and each branch needs a condition stated beside it, otherwise the second mark is not earned. The three headings the guideline looks for are a sequence, the possible outcomes, and the pathways followed.

items: (i) Gravitational collapse draws matter inward under the mutual attraction of its particles, and the falling matter converts gravitational potential energy into kinetic energy and then into heat, so the cloud contracts and its temperature rises. The rising temperature raises the kinetic energy of the particles and therefore the pressure they exert, and this outward pressure eventually balances the inward gravitational force, at which point the star stabilises on the main sequence.

(ii) $X$ lies on the red giant branch, so its core hydrogen is exhausted and it is now fusing helium into carbon and oxygen through the triple-alpha reaction at about $10^{8}\,\mathrm{K}$. $Y$ lies on the main sequence, so it is fusing hydrogen into helium, predominantly through the carbon-nitrogen-oxygen cycle with carbon acting as a catalyst. The two are similar in that both fuse lighter nuclei into heavier ones and both release energy; they differ in the fuel, the products, the core temperature and the reaction pathway.

(iii) Red giant, helium exhausted, core contracts and heats: either the outer layers are shed as a planetary nebula and the cooling carbon-oxygen core is left as a white dwarf, ending the sequence, or, if the star is of high mass, it becomes a supergiant, fuses elements up to iron, collapses and ends as a type II supernova leaving a neutron star, or collapses completely to a black hole.

content.text: (c)(i) Two marks, for features and characteristics of both processes. The inward process is gravitational collapse, which causes contraction: every particle in a cloud of gas attracts every other one, and the attraction of the outer layers on the inner ones compresses the cloud, so its radius decreases and its density increases. As the cloud contracts, gravitational potential energy is converted into kinetic energy of the falling matter and then, through collisions, into thermal energy, so the temperature rises steadily. The outward process is the pressure exerted by the hot particles, which causes expansion: as the temperature rises the average kinetic energy of the particles rises, and the pressure they exert on their surroundings rises as well. The two processes are in competition throughout. When the outward pressure of the hot core exactly balances the inward gravitational force, hydrostatic equilibrium is reached, contraction stops, and the star is born; the balance also fixes the star's radius and luminosity, which is why stars of a given mass settle at a particular point on the main sequence.

(c)(ii) Two marks for showing how the reactions at the two positions are similar and how they differ, or one mark for identifying the type of reaction at either or both. Reading the diagram, $Y$ lies on the main sequence in the hot, very luminous region at around spectral class B, while $X$ lies off the main sequence on the red giant branch, cooler at about spectral class K but with a high luminosity. The position on the diagram determines the stage of evolution and therefore the reaction. At $Y$ the star is on the main sequence, so it is fusing hydrogen into helium in its core; because the star is hot, the carbon-nitrogen-oxygen cycle dominates over the proton-proton chain, and in that cycle carbon acts as a catalyst, being used and regenerated as the cycle proceeds. At $X$ the star is a red giant, so the hydrogen in its core has been exhausted; the core has contracted under its own gravity and heated to roughly $10^{8}\,\mathrm{K}$, and the star is now fusing helium into carbon and oxygen through the triple-alpha reaction, in which four helium nuclei ultimately combine to form one carbon nucleus. The similarities are that both are fusion of lighter nuclei into heavier ones, both release energy because the products have a greater binding energy per nucleon, and both need enormously high temperature and density so that the nuclei can overcome their mutual electrostatic repulsion. The differences are the fuel, hydrogen against helium; the products, helium against carbon and oxygen; the core temperature, of order $10^{7}\,\mathrm{K}$ against $10^{8}\,\mathrm{K}$; and the pathway, the CNO cycle against the triple-alpha reaction.

(c)(iii) Two marks, one for a diagram that shows a sequence with the possible outcomes and the pathways followed, and one for a sequence or for correct information not in flowchart form. Draw the sequence as boxes joined by arrows with the two branches explicit. A red giant has exhausted core helium, so it first moves to the horizontal branch, where helium burns in a shell around an inert carbon-oxygen core, and then to the asymptotic giant branch, where helium and hydrogen burn in alternating shells and the star is a supergiant. From the asymptotic giant branch the path forks. The lower-mass branch, taken by stars of up to about eight solar masses, is that the outer layers are expelled as a planetary nebula, the remaining core cools and becomes a white dwarf, and the sequence ends there. The higher-mass branch, taken by stars above about eight solar masses, is that the core fuses elements heavier than helium up to iron, the star becomes unstable and explodes as a type II supernova, and the remnant is either a neutron star or, if the core mass is great enough, a black hole. Writing the mass condition beside each arrow is what earns the second mark, because the diagram has to show the pathways followed and not merely a list of stages.

A useful addition to any answer here is that elements heavier than iron cannot be formed by fusion in a star, because their binding energy per nucleon is lower than iron's, so such a reaction absorbs energy instead of releasing it; the heavier elements are made in supernovae and neutron-capture events instead.

content.text: Explain how observations of binary and variable stars can be used to infer physical properties of these stars.

This is a 6-mark explanation, so start by saying why inference is necessary at all: direct measurement in astronomy is very limited, so nearly everything known about stars is inferred from relationships between quantities that can be measured from the ground. That opening sentence is what the coherence mark is built on.

For binary stars work through the measurable quantities and what each yields. For a visual binary the period and the separation can both be measured, so ask what Newton's law of gravitation gives from those two. For an eclipsing binary ask what the drops in brightness tell you. For a spectroscopic binary ask what the Doppler shift of the lines reveals, and note that it works even when the two stars cannot be seen separately.

For variable stars, the essential fact is that a Cepheid's period of variation is directly related to its true luminosity. Follow the chain: period, then luminosity, then absolute magnitude, then the distance modulus with the measured apparent magnitude, and you have a distance to a star that cannot be measured any other way.

Measuring the period and separation of a visual binary gives the total mass from Kepler’s third law; Doppler shift reveals motion in spectroscopic binaries and eclipses in eclipsing binaries. For a Cepheid variable, the period gives the luminosity and hence the distance via the distance modulus.

Direct measurement in astronomy is limited, and most knowledge we have about stars is inferred, based on relationships between physical quantities. Binaries and variable stars can provide us with information in this way. Binary stars are pairs of stars that are orbiting around each other, which may not always be obvious. Visual binaries are binaries in which both stars can be seen using a telescope. In these cases we can measure the period of their motion and the distance between them (by trigonometric parallax). Using this information the total mass of the system can be determined; if the distance to the centre of mass of one star is known then individual masses can be determined. Measurement of changes in brightness can indicate when one moves into the shadow of the other, as in eclipsing binaries. Measurement of Doppler shift in spectroscopic binaries can reveal motion otherwise undetectable. Variations such as Cepheid variable stars show distinct variation of luminosity with time. If the period can be measured then luminosity can be determined, which can then be used to determine absolute magnitude. Since apparent magnitude can be measured, the distance modulus formula can be used to calculate its distance.

An atom of Carbon-12 has 6 protons and 6 neutrons in its nucleus. The mass of a Carbon-12 atom is 12.000 atomic mass unit. Show that the mass defect of one Carbon-12 atom is 0.097 atomic mass unit.

Describe the key features and components of the standard model of matter.

The standard model has families of particles: leptons that do not interact via the strong force; quarks that make up hadrons; and the particles that give rise to the interactions - gluons (strong), photons (electromagnetic), W and Z particles (weak) and the graviton (gravitational).

content.text: Use the work of TWO physicists to explain how the combination of ideas led to new directions in scientific thinking about atomic structure.
Choose two physicists whose work is complementary rather than competing - for example the experiment that revealed the nuclear structure and the theory that made that structure stable.
For each, state what they actually did or proposed, not just the name and the date.
The last mark is for the link: say what the combined ideas explained that neither of them explained on its own.

Rutherford’s gold foil experiment showed the atom has a small dense nucleus with empty space around it; Bohr’s model placed electrons in stable orbits that emit only when they change level. Together they explained the line spectra of hydrogen and opened the way to quantum models of the atom.

Rutherford’s experiment scattering alpha particles off gold foil led him to believe that the atom was made of a nucleus with a lot of empty space and electrons moving around the outside of the nucleus. Bohr had developed a theoretical model of the atom, based on a number of assumptions that were not readily obvious. This model included orbits in which electrons could exist without emitting radiation. Electrons would only emit or absorb radiation as they moved from one orbit to another. Rutherford’s work gave support to Bohr’s model while the two combined provided a new understanding by explaining the observed line spectra of hydrogen.

content.alt_text: Logarithmic graph of element size in units of $10^{-6}\,\mathrm{m}$ (from 0.001 to 100) against year from 1970 to 2020. Four data points lie on a straight line of negative gradient: about 300 in 1970, about 40 in 1980, about 5 in 1990 and about 0.7 in 2000.

content.text: The axis on this graph is a LINEAR size, not an area. Work out what happens to the number of devices that fit on a fixed area of silicon as that linear size falls, and separately what happens to the switching speed of each device.

The data points lie on a straight line on the LOG scale, so the size falls by a roughly constant factor per decade. Extend that line forward to 2040 and convert the intercept back into nanometres before you judge whether the prediction is physically possible.

(i) Reducing the linear size of the IC element transistors increases the number that can be fitted on a given area of silicon, as $1/(\text{linear size})^{2}$, and increases their speed, so processing and storage capability rose by many orders of magnitude over 1970-2000. (ii) Extrapolating the trend predicts an IC element size of about 0.1 nm in 2040; elements of this size are subject to quantum effects that are incompatible with the operation of current ICs, so alternative technology must be developed to replace current IC technology.

The straight line on the log axis means the element size falls by a roughly constant factor per decade: about 300, then 40, then 5, then 0.7, in units of $10^{-6}\,\mathrm{m}$ across 1970-2000. That is a reduction in linear size by a factor of more than 200.

The linear size of a transistor also sets how quickly it can charge and discharge, so smaller devices switch faster. Processing and storage capability of a computer is proportional to the number and the speed of the devices used to build it, so a linear size reduced by a factor greater than 200 raises the device count by a factor of order $10^{5}$ and adds a further gain from speed. The marking guidelines summarise this as an increase in computing performance of more than $10^{7}$ over the interval.

For the extrapolation, continue the same straight line on the log axis. Over 1970-2000 the size falls by about 2.6 decades in 30 years, so a further 40 years removes about 3.5 decades, taking $0.7$ down to of order $2\times10^{-4}$ in units of $10^{-6}\,\mathrm{m}$, that is roughly $0.1$ to $0.2\,\mathrm{nm}$. This is the value the marking guidelines give as about $0.1\,\mathrm{nm}$.

At that scale a transistor is only a few hundred electron wavelengths across, so electron confinement and quantum tunnelling dominate and the band-gap barrier that switches the device can no longer be controlled in the classical way. The physical principles behind the operation of current integrated circuits are therefore incompatible with elements of this size, which implies that alternative technology must be developed to replace current IC technology.

content.text: An ideal differential-input operational amplifier is connected into the following circuit.

content.alt_text: Inverting summing operational amplifier circuit. $V_{in}$ and $V_B = +1.0$ V each feed the inverting input through a 10 kΩ resistor; the two resistors and the summing junction are enclosed in a dashed box. A 100 kΩ resistor connects the output back to the inverting input. The non-inverting input is connected to ground.

content.text: An ideal op-amp is defined by three things: its gain, its input resistance and its output resistance. Get all three into your answer for the first mark.
Before calculating anything, identify the role of each resistor. The one running back from the output to the inverting input is not part of the input network.

For the transfer characteristic the closed-loop gain is fixed by the ratio of the feedback resistor to each input resistor, and BOTH inputs arrive at the inverting terminal, so both contribute to the output.

(i) Infinite (or very high) differential gain, infinite input resistance so that it does not load the source circuit, and zero output resistance so that the output signal does not depend on the load. (ii) It is the negative feedback resistor, returning a signal proportional to the output to the inverting input. (iii) It is the summing circuit, adding the two input signals with equal weighting. (iv) A straight line of gradient $-10$, that is $V_{out} = -10V_{in} - 10\,\mathrm{V}$, passing through $(V_{in} = 0,\ V_{out} = -10\,\mathrm{V})$ and $(V_{in} = -1.0\,\mathrm{V},\ V_{out} = 0)$.

With negative feedback an ideal op-amp holds its inverting input at the potential of the non-inverting input, which is grounded here, so the inverting input is a virtual earth and no current flows into either input terminal. All the current through each input resistor must therefore flow through the feedback resistor, and the summing rule follows.

The gradient of the transfer characteristic is the closed-loop gain, $-10$, so the line falls from left to right. Setting $V_{out} = 0$ gives $V_{in} = -1.0\,\mathrm{V}$, and setting $V_{in} = 0$ gives $V_{out} = -10\,\mathrm{V}$; those two points fix the line on the printed axes.

Two features of the answer are worth stating explicitly. The bias input $V_{B} = +1.0\,\mathrm{V}$ shifts the whole line down by $10\,\mathrm{V}$ without changing its gradient, which is the signature of a summing amplifier with equal weighting. And because the gradient is so large, a real amplifier saturates at its supply rails for input values more than a fraction of a volt away from the working point, so the ideal straight line is valid only over a small range; the idealisation is what allows the whole line to be drawn.

content.text: In recent years, torches using LEDs rather than incandescent bulbs have become commonly available.
Think of the LED as a diode: name the junction it is built from, and say what happens when a forward potential difference is applied to it.

For the comparison, the guidelines want any TWO of three points: electrical efficiency, mechanical robustness and lifetime. Choose two and, for each, say what it means for a torch that gets knocked about in a pocket.

(i) A p-n junction with metal contacts to an anode and a cathode. When a potential difference is applied, holes are injected into the anode and electrons into the cathode; they meet and recombine at the junction, emitting light of a wavelength characteristic of the semiconductor's energy gap. (ii) LEDs convert electric power into light much more efficiently, so the battery lasts far longer; they are mechanically robust where the incandescent filament is very fragile, so they survive being knocked; and their lifetime is much longer than that of an incandescent bulb, so the torch needs replacing far less often.

An LED is a two-layer semiconductor, p-type joined to n-type, with metal contacts so that a potential difference can be applied across the junction. Applying a forward potential difference injects holes into the p-type anode and electrons into the n-type cathode. Where they meet at the depletion region an electron falls from a higher energy level to a lower one, and the energy gap is released as a photon, so light is emitted with a wavelength set by the band gap of the chosen semiconductor. That is why different semiconductor materials give different coloured LEDs, and why the same effect is not produced in a reverse-biased junction.

For the comparison the marking guidelines accept any two of the following. LEDs convert electric power into light far more efficiently than a filament lamp, most of whose input energy becomes heat, so for the same battery the torch runs much longer. The LED is a solid-state device with no fragile filament to snap, so it tolerates being dropped or knocked, whereas a torch with an incandescent bulb fails after a single impact. The LED's lifetime is orders of magnitude longer than that of an incandescent bulb, so the torch needs far fewer replacements over its service life. Each of the three converts directly into a practical advantage in this application.

content.text: Advances in computer technology based on high-speed digital integrated circuits have had a huge impact on the design of electronics. However, analogue transducers still play an important role in many modern circuits.
Explain these statements, providing examples from modern electronics.
Split the response into two halves: what digital integrated circuits have achieved, and why they have not removed the need for transducers.

The marks come from named examples. Choose devices a student would recognise - a digital camera, a thermostat, a television, an MP3 player - and for each say exactly which analogue quantity has to be measured or produced.

Digital IC advances have raised processing and storage capability by many orders of magnitude and moved operations formerly done analogue into software, but a circuit must still measure and output analogue signals to interact with an analogue environment, e.g. the image sensor in a digital camera, an LDR setting exposure, a capacitive touch sensor in an iPod, or the speaker in an MP3 player.

Orders of magnitude increase in processing capacity. Many operations that were once performed using analogue circuits are now performed using digital computational techniques or in software. However, when the circuit must interact with its environment it must measure or output analogue signals because the environment is analogue in nature. Examples: a digital camera stores and processes image information digitally, however the level of light delivered through the lens to the image plane is an analogue quantity; without the analogue image sensor the digital processing capability of the camera is useless. A computer thermostat — temperature is an analogue quantity. A digital TV signal is converted to an analogue transmission, received as analogue, converted to digital, decoded and displayed. An LDR in a camera is used by the processor to determine the exposure time. An image sensor in a digital camera. A capacitive touch sensor in an iPod. A speaker in an MP3 player.
